items.content_excerpt: $ONDS Let’s look at CEO Eric Brock’s actual SEC filings. In June 2026, Brock received 4.5 million shares through his company stock compensation. Of the shares involved, 2,378,245 were sold to cover potential tax obligations associated with that compensation, according to the SEC filing. So how much does Brock still own? 3,583,010 common shares held directly. Another 1,153,625 shares held indirectly through Privet Ventures LLC. That’s 4,736,635 common shares retained in total. He also has 9 million additional restricted stock units (RSUs) company stock awards he is scheduled to receive over time through March 2029. Now here’s something to consider: Why would Brock necessarily need to buy more shares on the open market when he already has over 4.7 million common shares and another 9 million stock awards scheduled to be received over time? Look at the full picture: the filings, the remaining ownership, the business execution, and the financials. Facts over fear.

items.content_excerpt: $MSFT $GOOG $APLD Elon spent Sunday night talking about guppies. Tomorrow we hear from the whales. Microsoft buys capacity from a good chunk of the neoclouds he was warning about, Nebius and IREN included, and Google backstops billions of Fluidstack's lease obligations at Cipher and TeraWulf. What those two say about capacity tomorrow night lands directly on the companies supplying it. Two other things come first, power and money, and this group lives on both. GE Vernova reports before the open, and it makes the gas turbines a lot of the buildout is waiting on. It ended June with 116 gigawatts of backlog and reserved slots, and the longer that queue gets, the more capacity that already has power is worth. The Fed follows in the afternoon with a hold priced in and the argument already moved to December. This group has traded on the cost of money all summer, so I'll be listening to that press conference as closely as the calls. Microsoft guided Azure to about 45 percent growth in constant currency and keeps saying demand is ahead of capacity. It also has about $329 billion in leases that haven't started yet, mostly for data centers, which is a lot of somebody's future rent. Read its capex number twice before anyone sells a landlord over it. This year Microsoft stretched the useful life of its data centers from 15 years to 25, which means more new leases get booked as operating leases, outside reported capex. The rent is still owed, and a company that decides its buildings last twenty-five years is making my case for me. Google's numbers got a preview on Monday. Anthropic's S-1 showed at least $114.5 billion committed to Google through 2033, owed whether it uses the capacity or not, and it's nice when the customer files the receipts before the vendor reports. items.content_excerpt: Amazon is urging software engineers to use artificial intelligence more selectively, warning that token consumption and code generation are “deeply flawed” metrics for measuring AI adoption and productivity.
